Advisory, not diagnostic. Each finding states what was observed, why it stood out, which frames evidence it, and what to check next. None of them names a cause — that conclusion is yours to draw from the frames.

Complete v1 rule set: all 15 rules are implemented (R01 zero-window-stall, R02 syn-unanswered, R03 syn-rejected, R04 server-response-outlier, R05 rto-retransmission, R06 fast-retransmission, R07 out-of-order-not-loss, R08 asymmetric-loss, R09 reset-mid-transfer, R10 rtt-outlier, R11 dns-failure, R12 tls-handshake-failure, R13 pmtu-blackhole, R14 connection-churn, R15 capture-quality). These fifteen conditions are what this tool looks for; anything outside them was not examined, so a quiet result means these checks found nothing rather than that the capture is healthy.

Capture completeness

The capture-quality assessment covers snaplen truncation, the proportion of flows that began before the capture started, segments larger than the MTU (an on-host capture with offload enabled), and flows seen in one direction only. Timestamp resolution and multi-interface merges are not yet assessed. These figures describe what was read, not a verdict on whether the capture was adequate.

Checks not performed, and why

Rendered rather than dropped. A report that looks clean because half the checks never ran will close a ticket on a fault that is still live. This is the same coverage the application itself shows; the export carries it because a reader here has no other way to know what was left unexamined.

R04 · not assessed Not assessed: server response time for 4 server endpoints with fewer than 5 completed request/response exchanges. Percentiles over that few samples would not describe a distribution.
R10 · not assessed Not assessed: comparative network latency. 0 hosts had at least 3 flows with a usable round-trip measurement, and this check compares hosts against the others in the same capture, so fewer than 2 gives it nothing to compare.
R15 · not assessed Not assessed: anything comparing the two directions of a conversation. 1 of 5 flows were captured in one direction only, which usually means the capture point saw traffic going one way. Loss direction analysis is unavailable for those.
R15 · not assessed Not assessed: whether the capture host dropped packets before writing them. The classic pcap format has no field to record it, so this file cannot say either way. Packets dropped by the capturing machine look the same as packets lost on the network. If that distinction matters here, re-capturing in pcapng format would record the count.
R02 · note 1 connection attempt had not been answered when the capture ended, within 2.0s of the last frame. A reply may have arrived after the capture stopped, so these are not reported as unanswered.
R15 · note This file declares a capture size limit of 262,144 bytes per frame, and no frame reached it — nothing was clipped. Every packet was recorded in full.

Checks that ran

RuleNameWhat it looks for
R01zero-window-stallA receiver advertised a zero window having previously advertised non-zero, blocking the sender until a window update arrived.
R02syn-unansweredA connection attempt received no answer at all — no acceptance and no refusal — despite the client retrying.
R03syn-rejectedA connection attempt was answered with a refusal rather than an acceptance — the host is reachable, and nothing is listening on that port.
R04server-response-outlierA server:port took materially longer to begin responding than its peers in the same capture, with network round-trip time subtracted.
R05rto-retransmissionSegments were retransmitted after a timer-shaped quiet gap with no duplicate ACKs asking for them — the sender stalled waiting for a timeout.
R06fast-retransmissionSegments were retransmitted after three or more duplicate ACKs — packet loss the connection recovered from quickly.
R07out-of-order-not-lossSegments arrived out of sequence within milliseconds and in original transmission order by IP ID — reordering on the path, not packet loss.
R08asymmetric-lossRetransmission rate on one flow was at least five times higher in one direction than the other, with at least 20 retransmissions — loss is not symmetric.
R09reset-mid-transferA connection was terminated by reset while data was still moving, rather than closed cleanly once both sides were done.
R10rtt-outlierRound trips to one host took far longer than to every other host in the same capture, which usually reflects distance or a congested link rather than anything wrong with the host.
R11dns-failureName lookups went unanswered, came back as errors, or took a long time. A lookup happens before the connection it enables, so a slow one delays everything behind it and is often mistaken for application slowness.
R12tls-handshake-failureEncrypted connections failed to negotiate, took an unusually long time to set up, or presented a certificate close to expiry. A negotiation happens before any application data moves, so a failure here is not the application's fault.
R13pmtu-blackholeLarge segments were retransmitted repeatedly and never acknowledged while smaller ones on the same connection were delivered, which is the signature of a size limit on the path that nothing is reporting back to the sender.
R14connection-churnThe same client opened and closed many short-lived connections to one server:port instead of reusing them, paying the handshake cost each time.
R15capture-qualityReports what the capture itself may limit: flows already open when the capture began, connections seen in one direction only, packets the capture host dropped before writing them, frames clipped by a snaplen, and headers too damaged to be believed.
Generated offline. No network calls were made, no payload bytes appear in this report, and the capture file was opened read-only. Frame numbers refer to the capture as read by this tool and match Wireshark's numbering for the same file.
